Active anode material is the primary component for lithium-ion battery anodes, which enable the flow of electric charge. The material is therefore significant to the production of electric vehicles, consumer electronics, medical equipment and other applications. Importantly, the scope covers active anode material contained in a component of imported downstream products, such as batteries. [...] ## Scope

Active anode material, whether synthetic, natural or a blend of synthetic or natural; with or without coating; regardless of whether in powder, dry, liquid or any other form. Subject merchandise typically has a maximum size of 80 microns. Subject merchandise has an energy density of 330 milliamp hours per gram or greater and a degree of graphitization of 80% or greater. Subject merchandise can be referred to as “active anode material.” [...] Active anode material subject to the investigations may be classified under the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States (HTSUS) subheadings 2504.10.5000 and 3801.10.5000. Subject merchandise may also enter under HTSUS subheading 3801.90.0000. The HTSUS subheadings are provided for convenience and customs purposes only. The written description of the scope of the investigations is dispositive.

HTS classifications are listed in the scope of AD/CVD orders for convenience in assisting importers in determining whether a product may be subject to an AD/CVD order. However, the written description of the scope of the order is dispositive, not the HTS classification. Accordingly, the inclusion or exclusion of an HTS classification in the scope of an AD/CVD order does not determine whether a product falls under the scope of an AD/CVD order.

results.title: Vet a Product for Antidumping & Countervailing Duties | Dimerco
results.content:
When it’s unclear whether your product falls under an anti-dumping duty or countervailing duty order, you can request a formal scope ruling from the Department of Commerce. However, these rulings are technical, take time, and require precise documentation. 

Your customs broker or trade compliance expert can help build a strong case or advise when a ruling may not be worth pursuing. They can help you put together a strong, well-documented request, or tell you when to avoid one entirely. [...] If you’re importing into the United States, there is one thing you’ll want to avoid: surprise duties. Anti-dumping (AD) and countervailing duties (CVD) are tariffs imposed on goods that the U.S. government believes are unfairly priced or subsidized by foreign governments. These are not minor fees. In some cases, anti-dumping duty rates can exceed 100 percent and dramatically inflate your landed cost. [...] On the other hand, your product may still fall under the scope of a case even if its HTS code is not listed. The only way to know for certain is by carefully reviewing the scope language in the case documentation and comparing it against your product’s full description. This is another reason why working with a knowledgeable broker can make a big difference.
